analysis.one_liner: Caps patient out-of-pocket costs for high-priced specialty drugs at non-preferred brand levels.
analysis.headline: A bill limiting what insurers can charge patients for expensive specialty drugs — with 106 cosponsors from both parties — never got a hearing or a vote and died in a House committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Many insurance plans put expensive drugs for conditions like multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and cancer in a top 'specialty tier' and charge patients a percentage of the full price, which can run thousands of dollars a month. This bill would bar plans from charging more for specialty drugs than they charge for non-preferred brand drugs, using the lowest such tier if a plan has more than one. It was introduced by Rep. David McKinley with broad bipartisan support but was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients who need high-cost specialty drugs, such as people being treated for multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, HIV, and some cancers. Capping their cost-sharing at the non-preferred brand tier would lower what they pay at the pharmacy counter, particularly for plans that charge percentage-based coinsurance on specialty drugs [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group and individual health plans with tiered drug coverage from imposing cost-sharing — copayments or coinsurance — on specialty-tier drugs above the amount charged for non-preferred brand drugs [S2] [S3].
Uses the lowest non-preferred brand tier as the cap when a plan's formulary has more than one such tier, giving patients the tighter limit [S2] [S3].
Defines specialty tiers as the categories where patient cost-sharing exceeds that for generics, preferred brands, and non-preferred drugs, targeting the highest out-of-pocket exposure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and plan sponsors behind them would absorb the difference or spread it into premiums and other cost-sharing, since the bill restricts their ability to shift the cost of expensive specialty drugs onto the patients who need them [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay but does nothing to lower the underlying prices of specialty drugs; costs could resurface as higher premiums for all enrollees [S2] [S3].
It only applies to plans that use a formulary or tiered cost-sharing structure, and plans can redesign tiers, so some cost-shifting could continue in other forms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the patients who need specialty drugs, the benefit is direct and substantial: thousands of dollars a year in lower out-of-pocket costs. The honest tradeoff is that the bill restrains cost-shifting rather than drug prices, so part of the cost would likely be spread across premiums, and insurers could redesign benefit structures in response. On balance it targets a real affordability problem for a group facing the highest drug costs, without doing anything to fix the prices driving them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in March 2015, and no one ever scheduled a hearing or vote, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley introduced the Patients' Access to Treatments Act of 2015 on March 25, 2015, with 50 original cosponsors from both parties [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on March 25, 2015, and to the Subcommittee on Health on March 27, 2015 [S1] [S5].

It gathered 106 cosponsors — 89 Democrats and 17 Republicans — but the Energy and Commerce Committee took no further action and the bill never reached the House floor before the 114th Congress ended [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who fund plans came out ahead, keeping the freedom to place a large share of specialty drug costs on the patients who need those drugs. Patients on specialty medications gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. David McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 50 original cosponsors from both parties

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Fred Upton (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the two-year Congress

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 27, 2015 and took no action on it

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines heavily — 89 of 188 House Democrats and 17 of 247 House Republicans signed on — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the final outcome is a committee decision, not a roll call.

industries.note: The bill bars plans from charging more for specialty-tier drugs than for non-preferred brands, ending their main tool for shifting the cost of the most expensive drugs onto the patients who use them. Insurers could still respond with premiums or tier redesign, but their direct pricing flexibility would be curtailed.

Lower patient cost-sharing typically means fewer patients abandoning high-priced prescriptions, which supports sales for makers of specialty and biologic drugs. The bill leaves the drugs' list prices untouched, so the pricing system itself stays intact.
